title: Sundara Kāṇḍa: The Flight of Faith
body:
Sundara Kāṇḍa: The Flight of Faith

The Search in Lankā

Hanumān stood upon the mountain at the ocean’s edge, grown to his colossal stature, and gathered himself for the leap. He pressed down upon the mountain with his feet until the very rock groaned and sank beneath the force of his crouching, and then he sprang, and launched himself out over the sea, a hundred leagues of open water, flying through the air like a mountain hurled from a sling, like the very wind that was his father, streaking southward toward Lankā. It was a leap such as the world had never seen, and it is the leap that gives the whole Sundara Kāṇḍa its character, for this is the book of faith in flight, of devotion made mighty, of the impossible attempted and achieved out of pure love and loyalty.

And the leap was not unopposed, for the sea and its powers tested him as he flew, and the tellers give us three trials in the crossing, each with its own meaning.

First rose Mainaka, a golden mountain that dwelt beneath the sea, and Mainaka rose up out of the waters into Hanumān’s path, but not to bar him; rather, out of kindness, to offer him rest. The ocean had bid the mountain rise so that Hanumān, wearied by his great flight, might alight upon its golden peak and rest a while before going on. It was a gracious offer, and it would have been sweet to accept, but Hanumān would not. He touched the mountain lightly in courtesy, in acknowledgment of its kindness, but he did not stop, for he would not rest, would not pause, would not delay his errand for a moment while Sītā suffered and Rāma grieved. There is no rest, he said in effect, until the work is done. And he flew on. This is the first lesson of the crossing: that the servant of a great cause does not pause for his own ease, however kindly offered, while the work remains undone; that true devotion does not rest halfway.

Then came Surasā, a great sea-serpent, a demoness of the deep, and she rose to test him in another way, for she opened her vast mouth across his path and declared that he must pass through her jaws, that it was her boon that none should cross without entering her mouth. Here was not kindness but obstacle, and Hanumān met it not with force but with wit. He grew larger, and she grew larger to match him, widening her mouth; and he grew larger still, and she larger still; and then, suddenly, Hanumān shrank himself to a tiny size, darted into her open mouth and out again before she could close it, and so fulfilled the letter of her boon, having entered her mouth, without being caught by it. Surasā, satisfied and impressed, blessed him and let him pass. This is the second lesson: that not every obstacle is best met by force, that cleverness and quickness may accomplish what mere strength cannot, and that the wise servant knows when to grow great and when to grow small.

Then came Simhikā, a demoness who caught her prey by seizing its shadow upon the water and dragging it down, and she caught Hanumān’s shadow as he flew and began to drag him toward her to devour him. But Hanumān perceived the trick, and this one he met with force, for it was pure malice and admitted no other answer; he let her draw him toward her mouth, and then, growing suddenly, he tore into her and destroyed her from within, and flew on. This is the third lesson: that some evils are met neither with courtesy nor with cleverness but must simply be destroyed, and that the wise servant knows this too, and does not shrink from it when the moment calls.

So Hanumān crossed the sea, refusing rest, outwitting the obstacle, destroying the malice, and came at last to the far shore, to Lankā, and alighted upon its mountains, and looked down upon the golden city of the enemy.

And it was a formidable sight. Lankā was a fortress as much as a city, ringed with walls, watched by guards, its gates strong, its streets patrolled, a citadel of the demon power heavily guarded against exactly the kind of intrusion Hanumān now intended. To search it, Hanumān would have to enter it secretly, for a single vānara, however mighty, could not fight the whole host of Lankā at once, and his errand was to find Sītā, not to give battle. So Hanumān shrank himself down to a small size, the size of a cat, and waited for the cover of night, and under darkness he slipped toward the city to enter it unseen.

But even so he was challenged, for the city itself had a guardian spirit, Lankinī, the presiding deity of the fortress, and she saw the small intruding shape and rose to bar him at the gate, demanding to know who dared enter Lankā by stealth. And Hanumān struck her, a single blow, and it felled her, and in her falling she remembered an old prophecy: that when a vānara should overcome her, the doom of Lankā was at hand, for her defeat was the omen of the city’s fall. She let Hanumān pass, knowing that her overthrow was the sign that the end of Rāvaṇa’s golden city had begun. So Hanumān entered Lankā, and the very entering was an omen of its ruin, the first small crack in the fortress that would one day be brought wholly down.

And then began the long search through the city by night, and the tellers dwell on it, for it is a strange and vivid passage. Hanumān, tiny, unseen, crept through the sleeping city, through its streets and its gardens, and into its palaces, searching everywhere for Sītā. He passed through the great mansions of the demon lords, through halls of gold and chambers of luxury, searching room by room, for he did not know where in all that vast city the captive might be held. He came into Rāvaṇa’s own palace, the greatest of all, and searched through its splendours, through chamber after chamber of sleeping demons and heaped treasure and every kind of magnificence, looking always for the one face he sought.

And here the tellers give us a moment of great psychological delicacy, a moment that shows the fineness of Hanumān’s own soul. For in his search through Rāvaṇa’s palace, Hanumān came into the inner apartments where Rāvaṇa slept among his queens, and there he saw the demon king asleep, and around him his many wives, women of great beauty, and among them the chief queen, Mandodarī, whose beauty was such that for a single moment Hanumān’s heart leapt, thinking: can this be Sītā? Have I found her? But at once he checked himself, and corrected the thought, and was almost ashamed of it, reasoning: no, this cannot be Sītā; for Sītā, torn from her husband, grieving, faithful, would never be found sleeping peacefully in the luxury of the demon’s palace, adorned and at ease among his queens. The very peace and comfort of the sleeping woman proved she was not Sītā, for Sītā in her captivity and her grief could not possibly be at peace in such a place. And so Hanumān put the thought aside and searched on.

The tellers pause on this small moment because it shows us something true about Hanumān and about the discernment of the pure heart. He had felt, for an instant, the natural response of any eye to great beauty; but he corrected it at once, not by any rule imposed from without, but by his own understanding of what Sītā was, of what faithfulness and grief would look like, of the difference between the ease of the demon’s queen and the sorrow of the captive wife. His very love for Rāma, his understanding of Sītā’s devotion, told him that the beautiful sleeping woman could not be the one he sought, for Sītā’s whole being would be turned toward Rāma in grief, not sunk in the comfort of the enemy. It is the discernment of one who understands the heart he serves, and it kept Hanumān from error where a coarser searcher might have been deceived.

But nowhere in all the palace, nowhere in all the searched mansions of the great city, did Hanumān find Sītā, and as the night wore on toward its end his heart began to fail him, for he had searched so much and found nothing, and he feared that his whole great crossing might be in vain, that Sītā might be dead, or hidden where he could not find her, or not in Lankā at all. He had leapt the ocean and entered the fortress and searched the palaces, and still he had not found her, and despair crept toward him as the night thinned toward dawn. But he had not yet searched everywhere; there was still one place he had not looked, a grove apart from the palaces, a garden of ashoka trees within the palace grounds; and it was there, as the search seemed about to fail, that Hanumān would at last find what he had crossed the sea to seek.

Sītā in the Ashoka Park

Hanumān came at last to the Ashokavana, the grove of ashoka trees set apart within the palace grounds, and there, beneath a tree, he saw her, and he knew her at once, for grief has its own unmistakable form, and the woman he saw was the very image of faithful sorrow.

She was seated on the bare ground beneath the tree, and she was pale and thin and worn, her beauty dimmed by suffering as the moon is dimmed by cloud, her fine garments soiled and travel-worn, her ornaments gone, her hair unkempt, her whole aspect that of one who has grieved long and eaten little and slept less. She was surrounded by a ring of hideous rākshasīs, the demon- women set to guard and torment her, monstrous shapes that hemmed her in on every side; and in the midst of that ring of horror sat Sītā, small, worn, sorrowful, but unbroken, her spirit shining through her wasted body like a lamp through a thin screen.

Hanumān, hidden in the branches of the tree above her, looked down upon her and was moved to the depths of his soul, and the tellers dwell on the sight, for it is meant to wring the heart. Here was the queen of the great house of Ayodhyā, the beloved wife of Rāma, the daughter of a king, brought to this: seated on the bare earth in a demon’s garden, ringed by monsters, wasted with grief, a captive far from home and husband, not knowing whether Rāma lived, not knowing whether any help would ever come, enduring day after day the menaces of her keepers and the loneliness of her sorrow. The contrast between what she had been and what she was now, between the honoured queen and the wasted captive, was almost unbearable, and Hanumān, seeing it, wept in the branches for her suffering and for the wrong that had been done her.

And yet, and this is the thing the tellers most want us to see, Sītā in her wretchedness was not defeated. Her body was wasted, but her spirit was whole. For all her grief, for all her suffering, she had not yielded, had not despaired into surrender, had not for one moment wavered in her devotion to Rāma or in her refusal of Rāvaṇa. Her mind was fixed, wholly and unshakably, upon Rāma; her whole being was turned toward him in love and in longing; and no torment of her keepers, no menace, no offer, no length of captivity, had been able to move her from that fixed devotion by so much as a hair. She sat in the demon’s garden like a captive queen who was still, in the only way that finally mattered, entirely free, for the one thing her captors wanted, her consent, her yielding, her turning from Rāma to Rāvaṇa, they could not take and she would not give, and in that unbreakable refusal she was mistress of herself still, and stronger than all the power of Lankā arrayed to break her.

Let us honour Sītā’s strength here, for it is a different strength from Rāma’s or Hanumān’s, and no less great. Theirs is the strength of action, of the leap and the battle and the mighty deed. Hers is the strength of endurance, of holding fast, of remaining unbroken under a suffering she cannot end and a captivity she cannot escape. She cannot fight her way out; she cannot leap the ocean; she cannot destroy her guards. All the active powers of the story are denied her. She can do only one thing, and it is the hardest thing, and she does it perfectly: she can endure, and remain herself, and refuse to be broken, and keep faith, through suffering without end and without visible hope. And this endurance is not passive weakness but the most active kind of strength, the strength that holds a fortress when the walls are down and no relief is in sight, the strength that keeps faith in the dark with no promise that the dawn will ever come. Sītā’s fidelity in the Ashokavana, unwavering through all her suffering, is one of the great feats of the epic, as great in its way as Hanumān’s leap, and the story means us to see it so: that to endure faithfully is as heroic as to act mightily, and sometimes harder.

The tellers linger, too, on the particular image of her: like a crescent moon veiled by cloud, like a flame nearly smothered but not out, like a garden withered by drought that yet holds its life in the root waiting for rain. She was diminished but not destroyed; dimmed but not extinguished; her greatness was hidden under her suffering but it was there, entire, waiting only for deliverance to shine forth again. And Hanumān, watching her from the tree, understood that he had found not a broken woman to be pitied only, but a queen whose spirit had survived everything the enemy could do, and his pity was mixed now with a deep reverence, for he saw in her endurance a strength that matched, in its own way, the strength of Rāma himself.

But Hanumān did not yet reveal himself, for the moment was delicate and dangerous. Sītā was ringed by demon guards; a sudden appearance might alarm her into a cry that would bring the whole force of Lankā down upon them; and worse, Sītā, having been so cruelly deceived once already by Rāvaṇa’s disguise as an ascetic, might well take any stranger, even a friendly- seeming one, for another of the demon’s tricks, another shape-shifting torment sent to break her. Hanumān saw that he must approach her with the greatest care, must find a way to win her trust before he startled her, must prove himself a true messenger of Rāma and not another demon deception. And so he waited, hidden in the tree, watching, choosing his moment, and while he waited and watched, before he could find his opening, the moment was taken from him, for another came to the grove, and it was Rāvaṇa himself, come to press once more his suit upon the captive queen.

Hanumān, hidden above, would witness now, from his place in the branches, the confrontation between the demon king and the captive queen, and he would see with his own eyes the full measure of Sītā’s strength, her defiance of Rāvaṇa to his face, in the very hour of her helplessness, and the sight would show him, and shows us, exactly what manner of woman it was that Rāma had lost and that all this vast labour was to recover.

Rāvaṇa’s Solicitation

Rāvaṇa came to the Ashokavana in the deep of the night, in all his majesty, to press his suit upon Sītā once again, and Hanumān, hidden in the branches above, watched the whole confrontation, and it is one of the great scenes of the epic, a clash of wills between the mightiest of the demons and the most steadfast of women, in which the helpless captive proves stronger than the lord of the three worlds.

He came arrayed in all his splendour and his power, the ten-headed king, magnificent, terrible, adorned, the conqueror of gods, and he displayed himself before her in the full glory of his greatness, and he made his appeal, and his appeal was a mingling of temptation and menace, of offered glory and implied threat, all designed to break at last the will that had resisted him so long.

He offered her everything. Be my queen, he urged her, chief among all my queens, mistress of Lankā, of all its gold and all its power. What is Rāma to you now? A powerless exile, a wanderer in the forest, stripped of his kingdom, unable even to protect you, who could not prevent your taking and cannot accomplish your rescue. He is nothing; he has nothing; he can do nothing for you. Forget him. Turn to me, who am the lord of the three worlds, before whom the gods themselves tremble, who can give you every splendour and every pleasure and every power that exists. Be mine, willingly, and share my greatness; let go of your hopeless devotion to a broken exile, and be queen of the mightiest king in all creation. He heaped before her the whole treasure of his power and his wealth, all the temptation that the greatest king of the age could offer, urging her to abandon her lost husband and rise to be his consort.

And when temptation seemed to have no effect, he mingled it with menace, reminding her of her helplessness, of the length of her captivity, of the demon guards, hinting at the darker fate that awaited continued refusal, pressing upon her the hopelessness of her position, the folly of clinging to a devotion that could only bring her suffering, the wisdom of yielding to the inevitable while yielding could still be rewarded.

And Sītā answered him, and her answer is one of the glories of the epic, for the wasted captive, ringed by her tormentors, wholly in the power of the being who addressed her, answered the lord of the three worlds not with fear, not with pleading, not with the least tremor of weakness, but with a contempt so complete and a dignity so absolute that it reduced all his power and all his glory to nothing.

She would not even face him directly, the tellers say, but placed a single blade of grass upon the ground between them, and addressed her words as if to the grass, so as not to dignify the demon with her direct regard, a gesture of the most eloquent contempt, treating the mightiest king of the age as beneath her notice, as something to be addressed only through an intermediary blade of grass. And through this contempt she spoke her defiance.

Do not imagine, she told him, that your power or your wealth or your glory is anything to me. Compared to the virtue of Rāma, all your greatness is as dust, as this blade of grass, less than nothing. You call him a powerless exile; you do not understand what he is; and you will understand it, to your ruin, when he comes. For he will come. He will cross your ocean and break your city and destroy you and all your demon host, and he will take me back with honour, and your golden Lankā will be ash and your ten heads will roll in the dust, and all this because of the folly you have committed in taking me. You have not captured a prize; you have embraced your own destruction; you have signed the doom of your city and your race by this one act of lust and pride. My heart belongs to Rāma, wholly and forever, in life and beyond it, and no power of yours can take it or turn it or touch it. I would not be your queen if you offered me the sovereignty of all the worlds. Release me, and beg Rāma’s forgiveness, and you may yet save something from the ruin you have called down; keep me, and you and all your kingdom will perish. That is my answer, demon, and it will not change though you keep me here till the end of the world.

It was magnificent, and it was fearless, and it was spoken by a captive to her captor, by the helpless to the all-powerful, and its power lay precisely in that: that Sītā had nothing, could do nothing, was wholly in Rāvaṇa’s grip, and yet she was not conquered, could not be conquered, met his whole power with a contempt that his whole power could not touch. She had no weapon but her defiance, and it was enough, for it was the one thing he could not overcome. He could imprison her body; he could not bend her will. He could threaten and tempt and menace; she answered with contempt. All his greatness broke against her steadfastness like a wave against a rock, and the rock did not move.

Let us understand what the story is showing us in this confrontation, for it is one of its deepest points. Rāvaṇa has every kind of power: strength, wealth, sovereignty, the conquest of gods, the mastery of the three worlds. Sītā has no power at all, in the worldly sense; she is a captive, wasted, guarded, helpless. And yet in the confrontation it is Sītā who is strong and Rāvaṇa who is, at the root, weak, for all his power cannot get him the one thing he wants, and her powerlessness cannot be made to yield the one thing she guards. This is the story’s great reversal of what strength and weakness mean: that the truest strength is not the power to compel others but the power to remain oneself, unbroken, faithful, whole, under every compulsion; and that the truest weakness is not helplessness but the ungoverned wanting that makes even the mighty a slave to what they cannot have. Rāvaṇa, lord of the three worlds, is enslaved to his lust for a woman who despises him; Sītā, his captive, is free in the only way that finally matters, mistress of the one thing no one can take from her. And Rāvaṇa left the grove that night defeated, as he was always defeated in these encounters, raging, having gained nothing, having been answered with contempt by the one being in all his conquered worlds that he could not conquer.

And Hanumān, watching from the tree, had seen it all, and his heart was full, for he had seen now with his own eyes the full measure of Sītā’s greatness, the unbreakable fidelity, the fearless defiance, the strength that endured everything and yielded nothing. He understood now, more deeply than any report could have told him, what manner of queen it was that Rāma had lost, and why the whole world was being moved to recover her, and he was more resolved than ever to bring her comfort and to carry to Rāma the news that his Sītā lived and had kept faith and waited, unbroken, for her rescue. He had only to find the moment, now, to reveal himself to her without terror, and to give her the sign that would prove him Rāma’s true messenger, and bring, at last, the first ray of hope into the long darkness of her captivity.

First Among the Astute

When Rāvaṇa had gone, raging and defeated, he left orders with the demon guards, the rākshasīs who ringed Sītā, to redouble their torments, to break her by cruelty since he could not win her by temptation, to threaten and menace her without cease until her spirit gave way. And the demon-women fell to their work, crowding around the captive queen, threatening her with death, with devouring, with every horror, trying by sheer weight of menace to terrify her into yielding. And Sītā, worn and alone, ringed by these monstrous shapes shrieking their threats, sank toward the depths of despair, and even her great strength was sorely tried, for there is a limit to what any soul can bear, and the relentless cruelty of her keepers pressed her hard.

But among the demon-women who guarded her, there was one who was different, and her name was Trijaṭā, and she was old, and wise, and though a rākshasī by birth she had a righteous heart, and she had come, watching Sītā’s suffering and steadfastness, to pity and even to reverence the captive queen. And in the very hour when the other demon-women pressed their cruelty hardest, Trijaṭā intervened, and she did it in a way that turned the whole mood of the grove, for she had had a dream, a powerful and prophetic dream, and she now recounted it to the others, and its telling changed everything.

Stop your cruelty, Trijaṭā told the demon-women, and hear the dream I have had, for it is a warning to us all. And she told them her dream, and it was full of omens, and every omen pointed one way: to the triumph of Rāma and the doom of Lankā. She had seen, in her dream, Rāma, radiant, mounted upon a great white celestial elephant, or by other tellings a heavenly chariot, clad in shining white, coming in glory; and she had seen Sītā, reunited with him, seated at his side, honoured, restored, delivered. And she had seen, against these bright images, the omens of ruin for Lankā: she had seen Rāvaṇa fallen, clad in red, smeared with oil, dragged southward toward the region of death, tumbling into a pit of filth and darkness; she had seen the demons in disarray and terror; she had seen the golden city of Lankā given over to flames, burning, consumed, its glory turned to ash. Every image of the dream spoke the same message: Rāma triumphant, Sītā delivered, Rāvaṇa destroyed, Lankā burned.

Do not torment her, Trijaṭā warned the other demon-women, for this dream is true, and it tells us plainly what is coming. This captive whom you threaten is destined for deliverance and for glory; her husband is coming, and he will triumph, and he will destroy all of us who have wronged her. If you are wise, you will not add to her sufferings now, but will rather seek her goodwill, that she may protect you when her hour of triumph comes, as it surely will. The doom of Lankā is written; I have seen it; and the part of wisdom is to fear it, and to treat this queen not with cruelty but with the respect due to one whose deliverance is certain and whose husband will soon be our destroyer.

And the dream, and Trijaṭā’s warning, worked a change upon the demon- women, for even the wicked fear omens, and even the cruel grow cautious when they are shown their coming ruin. The threatening subsided; the cruelty eased; the demon-women, shaken by the dream and its clear prophecy of Lankā’s fall, drew back from their torment of Sītā, and the grove grew quieter, and Sītā was granted, through Trijaṭā’s intervention, a respite from the worst of her keepers’ menace.

There is a purpose in this episode beyond the mere easing of Sītā’s suffering, and the tellers dwell on it, for Trijaṭā’s dream serves the story in several ways at once. It brings comfort to Sītā in her darkest hour, for she too heard the dream, and its prophecy of Rāma’s coming and her own deliverance was balm to her despairing heart, a promise, spoken even by one of the enemy, that her faith was not in vain and her rescue was truly coming. It shows us that even among the demons, even in the very household of Rāvaṇa, there were those whose hearts could perceive the truth and incline toward the right, that wickedness was not total even in Lankā, that a righteous soul could exist even among the rākshasas and could pity the innocent and foresee the justice that was coming. And it sounds, for us who read, a note of assurance amid the darkness, a promise that the long night of Sītā’s captivity and the whole tragedy of the abduction would end in deliverance and in justice, that Rāma would come and Rāvaṇa would fall and Sītā would be restored, exactly as the dream foretold.

Let us mark, too, the particular kind of wisdom that Trijaṭā represents, for the chapter’s name honours it: the wisdom that reads the signs, that perceives which way the deeper currents of justice are running, that knows how to align itself with the truth even against the will of its own kind. Trijaṭā was a rākshasī, born among the enemies of Rāma, bound to the household of the demon king; and yet she saw the truth that her king in his pride could not see, that Rāma would triumph and Lankā would fall, and she had the wisdom and the courage to say so, and to counsel mercy, and to incline toward the right even at the risk of her own kind’s displeasure. It is a rare and valuable wisdom, this ability to see past the loyalties of birth and faction to the deeper truth of where justice lies, and to act on it; and Trijaṭā, alone among the demon-women, had it, and used it, and so became, in the midst of the enemy’s household, an unexpected friend to the captive queen and an unexpected servant of the truth. She is one more of the story’s quiet helpers, the righteous soul in an unexpected place, and her dream and her mercy are one more link in the long chain of graces by which Sītā was sustained and Rāma’s cause advanced.

So the grove grew quiet, and Sītā, comforted a little by the dream of her coming deliverance, sat on in her captivity with a spark of new hope kindled in her despair. And now, at last, with the demon-women subdued and the grove grown still, the moment had come for which Hanumān, hidden in the tree above, had been waiting: the moment to make himself known to Sītā, gently, carefully, and to give her the sign that would prove him no demon’s trick but the true and longed-for messenger of Rāma.

Sītā Comforted

The moment had come, and Hanumān approached it with all the care its delicacy required, for he understood that a wrong move here could undo everything. Sītā had been deceived once by a demon in disguise, and the wound of that deception was raw; if Hanumān revealed himself suddenly, in his vānara form, a talking monkey in a tree, she might well take him for another of Rāvaṇa’s shape-shifting torments, another cruel trick to raise her hopes and dash them, and she might cry out, or despair, and the whole errand would be ruined. Hanumān had to win her trust before he claimed it, to soften the ground before he stepped on it, to make himself known so gently and so truly that she could believe, past all her wariness, that here at last was a real friend.

So he began not by declaring himself but by speaking, softly, from his hiding place in the branches, of Rāma. In a low and gentle voice, so as not to startle her, he began to tell the story of Rāma, to sing his praises, to recount the tale of the prince of Ayodhyā, his birth, his virtues, his exile, his loss of Sītā, his grief, his alliance with the vānaras, his search. He let the beloved story fall into Sītā’s ears like a gentle rain, speaking of Rāma with such knowledge and such love that the words themselves carried their own proof, for who but a true friend of Rāma would speak of him so, and know so much, and love him so plainly?

And Sītā, hearing from somewhere above her the name of Rāma spoken with love, hearing his whole story told tenderly by an unseen voice, was at first amazed, and then wary, and then, slowly, moved past her wariness toward a trembling hope. Who spoke so of Rāma, here, in the demon’s garden? Could it be true? Or was it another trick? She looked up, and saw at last the small vānara form in the branches, and her wariness flared, for what was this creature, and was it another of Rāvaṇa’s illusions? But the words it had spoken, the love in them, the true knowledge of Rāma, pulled against her fear, and she hardly dared to believe and hardly dared to disbelieve.

And Hanumān, seeing her caught between hope and fear, gave her the proof, the one unanswerable sign that no demon’s trick could counterfeit. He came down, gently, humbly, making himself small and unthreatening, and he spoke to her directly now, telling her who he was: the messenger of Rāma, sent to find her, come across the ocean to bring her word and hope. And to prove it, he brought out the token that Rāma had given him for exactly this moment: Rāma’s signet ring, the ring from Rāma’s own hand, which Sītā knew, which she could not fail to know, which no demon could have counterfeited. He gave her the ring.

And when Sītā took the ring into her hands, and saw that it was truly Rāma’s, truly the ring she knew from his own finger, the last of her wariness broke and fell away, and the truth flooded in upon her: that this was real, that this was a true messenger, that Rāma lived, that Rāma knew where she was, that help had come at last across the impossible ocean, that she was not forgotten, not abandoned, not alone in the dark forever. The ring in her hands was the proof of everything her captivity had made her fear to hope: that Rāma was alive, that he grieved for her and sought her, that rescue was truly coming.

And the flood of it overwhelmed her. After all the long months of captivity, of grief, of menace, of not-knowing, of holding on with no visible reason to hope, the sudden certainty that Rāma lived and that his messenger stood before her broke through all her hard-held composure, and Sītā wept, and her tears were not the tears of despair that had been her companions so long but the tears of a hope almost too great to bear, the release of all the pent grief and longing of her captivity into a single overwhelming moment of restored hope. She held the ring, and she wept, and she asked Hanumān a thousand things at once: Did Rāma truly live? Was he well? Did he grieve for her? Was he coming? How had this messenger crossed the ocean? When would rescue come? All the dammed-up longing of her heart poured out in questions, and the messenger’s coming was to her as water to one dying of thirst, as light to one long in darkness, the first pure joy she had known since the day she was taken.

Let us feel the sweetness of this moment, for the story means us to, and it has earned it. We have followed Sītā through her taking, her captivity, her grief, her unbreakable endurance, her defiance of Rāvaṇa, her despair under the demon-women’s cruelty; we have seen her hold on with no reward, keep faith with no visible reason, endure and endure and endure. And now, at last, comes the first ray of light, the first reward of all that faithful endurance: the certain knowledge that Rāma lives and seeks her and is coming, brought to her across the ocean by a faithful friend. It is the turning of her long night toward its dawn, the first breaking of the darkness that had held her so long, and the joy of it, breaking through her long-held grief, is one of the tenderest things in the whole telling. Her faith, held so long in the dark, was vindicated at last; the deliverance she had defiantly promised Rāvaṇa, and half-feared to hope for herself, was truly coming; and the messenger of it sat before her with her husband’s ring in her hands and her husband’s love in his words.

And Hanumān, for his part, was filled with joy to have found her, to have brought her comfort, to have lifted, even a little, the terrible weight of her captivity. This was the fruit of his great leap, the purpose of his whole crossing: not yet her rescue, for that would take the army and the war, but this, the finding of her, the bringing of hope, the assurance to the grieving captive that she was not forgotten and that help was on its way. He had crossed the ocean for this moment, and it was worth every league of the crossing, to see the light of hope break at last across the worn face of the captive queen, and to know that he would carry back to Rāma the news that would end his grief: that Sītā lived, and had kept faith, and waited, unbroken, for her rescue.

There remained now the practical matters, the questions of how and when the rescue would come, and Sītā would have counsel to give and a token to send, and there was the question, too, of whether Hanumān might simply carry her away himself, then and there, and spare the whole labour of the war. All this remained to be spoken of between them in the grove. But the great thing was done: Sītā was found, and Sītā was comforted, and the long darkness of her captivity had, at last, been pierced by the light of certain hope.

Sītā and Hanumān

When the first joy of the meeting had passed, there were things to be settled between them, and the conversation that followed reveals Sītā’s greatness once more, and turns upon a question of duty and dignity that she answers with a wisdom worthy of Rāma himself.

For Hanumān, seeing her suffering, and being who he was, mighty beyond measure, able to grow to a colossal size and to leap the ocean, made her an offer that must have been tempting past words. Why wait, he said in effect, for the army and the war and all the long labour of the rescue? Why should you endure this captivity a day longer than you must? I am strong enough; I can grow great; climb upon my back, and I will carry you across the ocean this very hour, back to Rāma, and end your captivity now, tonight, and spare you all further suffering and spare Rāma all further grief. Let me take you home. I have the strength; the thing can be done; you need not remain in this terrible place another day.

It was a real offer, and Hanumān had the power to make it good, and it would have ended Sītā’s suffering at once. And Sītā considered it, and she declined it, and her reasons are the heart of this chapter, and they show the depth of her understanding of dharma and of her own dignity.

She declined it, first, on a point of dignity and propriety that meant much to her. To be carried away upon the back of another male, she said, to let another man’s body bear her, even in rescue, even in so pure a cause, would be a thing that touched her honour and her vows as Rāma’s wife. She was devoted to Rāma alone; her person was Rāma’s; and to be borne away clinging to the body of another, however faithful a servant he was, was a familiarity that her fidelity would not easily permit. It was a fine and perhaps a severe scruple, but it was hers, and it flowed from the absolute purity of her devotion, and she held to it.

But she declined it, second, for a deeper reason, a reason of dharma that went beyond her own person to the honour of Rāma and of his whole line, and this is the argument the tellers most admire. If I were to escape in secret, she said, carried away by stealth in the night, then Rāma would be robbed of something that is his by right: the right to come himself, to defeat the demon who wronged him, to avenge the insult to his wife and his honour in open battle, and to take me back with his own hand, openly, in triumph. For consider what my abduction was: it was an insult, a challenge, a wrong done to Rāma and to the whole house of the Raghus, and such a wrong demands to be answered, not evaded. If I am smuggled out by a servant’s stealth, the wrong is not answered; it is merely undone; and Rāvaṇa is left unpunished, and the insult unavenged, and the honour of Rāma’s line unrestored. But if Rāma comes himself, and crosses the ocean, and meets Rāvaṇa in battle, and defeats him, and takes me back by the strength of his own arm, then the wrong is answered as a wrong must be answered, the insult is avenged, the demon is punished, and the glory of the Raghuvamsha, stained by my abduction, is washed clean and made bright again. It is not enough that I be rescued; it matters how I am rescued; and the only rescue that satisfies dharma and restores honour is the open victory of Rāma over Rāvaṇa in battle. Therefore I will not be carried away by stealth. I will wait. Let Rāma come, and conquer, and take me back with honour, so that the glory of his house remains untarnished.

Let us weigh what Sītā chose here, for it was a hard choice and a great one. She chose to remain in captivity, to endure more suffering, to prolong her own ordeal and Rāma’s grief, rather than accept an escape that would have ended her suffering at once but would have compromised the deeper demands of dharma and honour. She had every reason, every excuse, to accept Hanumān’s offer; no one could have blamed her for grasping at deliverance after all she had endured; and she refused it, deliberately, out of a clear understanding that some things matter more than the ending of suffering, that honour and dharma and the proper answering of a wrong are worth even the price of continued captivity. It is the same quality we have seen in Rāma, the willingness to choose the harder right over the easier relief, the refusal to evade the full demands of duty even when evasion is offered and would be forgiven; and Sītā shows it here as purely as Rāma ever showed it, and the tellers set the two of them side by side in this, husband and wife matched in their fidelity to the highest law even at the cost of their own suffering.

There is a further wisdom in her choice, too, a care for Rāma’s own greatness. For Sītā understood that to deny Rāma the chance to rescue her himself would be, in a way, to diminish him, to rob him of his rightful triumph, to treat him as one who needed his wife smuggled out by a servant because he could not win her back himself. Her refusal was, at its heart, an act of faith in Rāma and of care for his honour: a declaration that she trusted him to come, that she wanted him to have the victory that was his due, that she would rather suffer longer and be rescued by his open triumph than be delivered sooner in a way that lessened him. It was love that refused the easy escape, love that chose to wait for the beloved’s proper victory rather than accept a lesser deliverance, and it is one of the most moving things in all Sītā’s moving story.

So it was settled: Sītā would wait; Rāma would come; the rescue would be by open battle and not by stealth. And to seal the arrangement and to send her own token back to Rāma, as he had sent his ring to her, Sītā gave Hanumān a jewel of her own, the Chūḍāmaṇi, the crest-jewel she had worn in her hair, a precious ornament that Rāma would know, that would prove to him beyond doubt that Hanumān had truly found her and spoken with her, that she lived and kept faith and waited. As Rāma’s ring had proved Hanumān true to Sītā, so Sītā’s crest-jewel would prove Hanumān’s report true to Rāma, and would carry to her husband, across the ocean, the touch of her own hand and the token of her unbroken love. Hanumān received the jewel reverently, and treasured it, for it was the sign of his errand’s success and the proof he would carry home.

And with the jewel given and the counsel spoken and the arrangement sealed, Hanumān’s errand of finding was complete. He had crossed the ocean, entered the fortress, found the captive, comforted her, proved himself true, received her counsel and her token. There remained only to return, to carry back across the sea the news that would end Rāma’s grief and set the army in motion. But Hanumān, before he left, resolved to do one thing more, a thing not strictly required of a messenger, but that his own bold heart prompted: he would test the strength of Lankā, would give the demons a taste of what was coming, would strike a blow that would announce to Rāvaṇa that his golden city was no longer safe. And so, his gentle errand of comfort done, Hanumān prepared to turn from messenger into warrior, and to set the enemy’s garden, and soon the enemy’s city, ablaze.

Inviting Battle

His errand of finding was done, but Hanumān did not leave at once. He was, beneath his gentleness and his wisdom, a warrior, and a bold one, and he saw an opportunity that his bold heart could not let pass. He had found Sītā; he had comforted her; he had her token; he could have leapt back across the ocean that very hour with his news. But he reasoned that there was more he could usefully do before he left, and the reasoning was sound: he could test the strength of Lankā, could provoke the demons into revealing their forces, could gauge the enemy Rāma’s army would have to face, and, not least, could strike a blow that would announce to Rāvaṇa, in a way that could not be ignored, that his golden city was no longer the untouchable fortress he imagined it to be.

So Hanumān, the gentle messenger, became Hanumān the destroyer, and he began by wrecking the very grove in which he stood. The Ashokavana was Rāvaṇa’s pleasure-garden, a place he cherished, and Hanumān, grown great again, tore through it, uprooting its trees, smashing its pavilions, ruining its beauty, laying waste the demon king’s beloved garden in a storm of destruction, sparing only the one tree beneath which Sītā sat, and the ground immediately around her, so that she should not be harmed or frightened by the havoc. He made of the lovely grove a wreckage, deliberately, as a challenge, as a declaration, as a way of forcing the demons to come out and fight and so reveal themselves.

And come out they did. The demon guards, seeing their king’s garden being torn apart by a single monstrous vānara, raised the alarm, and the warriors of Lankā came pouring out to deal with the intruder, and Hanumān met them, and destroyed them. Wave after wave of demon warriors came against him, and he broke them, fighting with the uprooted trees and the pillars of the ruined pavilions and his own colossal strength, slaying the guards, scattering the soldiers, showing the whole city the terrible power of a single servant of Rāma.

The alarm mounted, and greater warriors were sent against him, and still Hanumān prevailed, and at last the demons brought word to Rāvaṇa himself that a mighty vānara had entered the city, found the captive, wrecked the royal garden, and was slaughtering the warriors sent against him. And Rāvaṇa, enraged and alarmed, sent out his own champions, his greatest fighters, and among them, at last, his own son. For the fighting drew in Aksha, or Akshakumāra, one of Rāvaṇa’s sons, a prince of the demons, a warrior of great prowess, and he came against Hanumān with the full force of his royal strength, and the combat between them was fierce and worthy, for Aksha was no common soldier but a mighty demon prince. But Hanumān was more than a match for him. They fought, and Hanumān, for all the young demon’s valour, overpowered him and slew him, killing Rāvaṇa’s own son before the eyes of the horrified city.

The killing of Aksha was a grave blow and a grave provocation, and the story means us to feel its weight, for now Hanumān had not merely wrecked a garden and slain some guards; he had killed a prince, a son of Rāvaṇa himself, and the war that was coming had drawn its first royal blood, and drawn it in the very heart of Lankā, by a single intruder. It was a demonstration of power that shook the whole city: that one servant of Rāma, sent merely to find the captive, could enter the impregnable fortress, wreck the royal garden, slaughter the warriors, and slay a prince of the blood, and still stand unconquered in the midst of the enemy’s capital. If a single messenger could do this, the demons must have begun to wonder, with a cold dread, what the master of such a servant, and the army of such servants, would do when they came.

Let us mark what Hanumān was doing here, for it was deliberate and it was strategic, and it shows a side of him beyond the gentle devotee. He was, in effect, delivering a message written in destruction: a message to Rāvaṇa and to all Lankā that their city was not safe, that their power was not invincible, that the force which had produced this single overwhelming warrior was coming, and that the golden fortress they had thought impregnable had been entered and wrecked and bloodied by one being alone. It was psychological warfare of the boldest kind, meant to sow dread in the enemy, to shake their confidence, to make them fear what was coming; and it was reconnaissance, too, for by provoking the demons into battle Hanumān learned their strength, tested their warriors, gauged the forces Rāma’s army would face. The wrecking of the grove and the slaying of Aksha were not mere destruction; they were a message and an assessment both, the work of a warrior who was also a strategist, using his own single overwhelming power to prepare the ground for the war to come.

But Hanumān had provoked the whole strength of Lankā now, and the demons, having lost a prince, would send against him a warrior greater than any yet, the mightiest of all Rāvaṇa’s sons, the one champion whose power might match even the son of the wind. For Rāvaṇa, hearing that Aksha was slain and the city in uproar, turned at last to his greatest son, the terror of the gods, the wielder of the most fearsome weapons in all the demon armoury, and sent him out to take or kill the intruder. And against this one, Hanumān would face a truly formidable foe, and would meet, at last, a weapon he chose not to resist.

The Terrible Envoy

The son whom Rāvaṇa now sent against Hanumān was Indrajit, and he was the greatest of all the demon warriors, greater even than his father in the arts of war, and his very name told his stature, for Indrajit meant Conqueror of Indra, and he had earned it by defeating Indra himself, the king of the gods, in battle, a feat that placed him among the mightiest beings in all creation. He was a master of sorcery and of the celestial weapons, able to fight from concealment, wrapped in illusion, wielding powers that few in any world could withstand. Against such a foe, even Hanumān faced a true and formidable test.

They fought, and the combat was tremendous, the greatest that Hanumān had yet faced, for Indrajit was no mere warrior to be overpowered but a master of the deepest arts of war, and the two of them, the son of the wind and the conqueror of Indra, contended with a fury that shook the city. And for all Hanumān’s power, Indrajit could not be easily overcome, nor could he easily overcome Hanumān, and the battle raged on, neither able to master the other by ordinary force.

And so Indrajit turned to the ultimate weapon, the Brahmāstra, the mightiest of all the celestial missiles, the weapon named for Brahmā the creator himself, against which there was no defence in all the worlds, the supreme astra whose power nothing could withstand. He invoked it, and he loosed it at Hanumān, and the Brahmāstra took hold of the son of the wind and bound him.

Now here the story does a subtle and important thing, and it turns on Hanumān’s own choice, and we must understand it rightly. The Brahmāstra was irresistible; nothing could withstand it; when it bound Hanumān, he was held. But the tellers are careful to say that Hanumān, who through his father the wind-god and his own great power had a measure of protection even against the Brahmāstra, could perhaps have resisted or broken free of it, or at least that he was not held wholly against his will. Rather, Hanumān chose to submit to it. He recognized the Brahmāstra for what it was, the weapon of Brahmā, a sacred and supreme power, and out of reverence for Brahmā, out of respect for the sanctity of that highest of weapons, he chose not to defy it but to honour it by submitting, allowing himself to be bound. And there was strategy in his choice as well as reverence, for Hanumān saw that being captured and brought before Rāvaṇa would give him something he could not otherwise obtain: an audience with the demon king himself, a chance to see the enemy face to face, to gauge him, and to deliver to him, in his own court, a warning and a challenge from Rāma.

So Hanumān allowed himself to be bound by the Brahmāstra, submitting where he might have resisted, and this is worth pausing on, for it shows a quality in him beyond mere power: the wisdom to yield at the right moment, the reverence to honour a sacred weapon even from an enemy’s hand, and the strategic vision to turn his own capture into an opportunity. A lesser warrior would have measured his greatness only by his refusal to be taken; Hanumān measured his by knowing when to submit, and to what, and to what end. His submission to the Brahmāstra was not weakness but a higher kind of strength, the strength that serves a purpose larger than the display of its own power, that accepts even capture when capture serves the cause better than resistance would.

But then a curious thing happened, and it is characteristic of the way the world treats even its sacred things carelessly once the first moment has passed. When Hanumān had been bound by the Brahmāstra and taken by the demons, they were not content with the binding of the sacred weapon alone; not understanding, or not trusting, the completeness of the Brahmāstra’s hold, they bound him further with ordinary ropes, coarse material bonds, heaping physical cords upon the captive to make doubly sure of him. And the moment they did so, the moment they added their ordinary ropes to the sacred binding, the Brahmāstra’s power was released, for such was the nature of that weapon, that it would not share its hold with lesser bonds, and would depart the moment cruder cords were added. So by their own clumsy overcaution the demons freed Hanumān from the one binding that truly held him, leaving him held only by ordinary ropes that his strength could break at any moment he chose.

But Hanumān did not break them, not yet, for the ropes served his purpose: they would carry him, as a bound captive, into the presence of Rāvaṇa, into the very court of the demon king, which was exactly where Hanumān now wished to go. He let himself be led, bound and seemingly helpless, though he could have freed himself in an instant, through the streets of Lankā and into the great assembly-hall of Rāvaṇa, playing the part of the captured intruder, biding his time, so that he might stand before the lord of the demons and look upon him and speak to him the warning he had come, in part, to deliver. The terrible envoy of Rāma, mightiest of the vānaras, slayer of Aksha, wrecker of the royal garden, was brought bound before the throne of Rāvaṇa, and the demon king and the servant of Rāma at last faced one another, and the confrontation that followed would show Rāvaṇa, in the person of a single bound captive, the spirit of the enemy that was coming to destroy him.

Hanumān Bound

They brought Hanumān bound into the great assembly-hall of Rāvaṇa, and it was a place designed to overawe, and the tellers describe its terrible splendour, for Rāvaṇa’s court was among the wonders of the three worlds. It blazed with gold and gems; its pillars rose vast and gleaming; its hall was thronged with the lords and warriors of the demon race, mighty and terrible in their arrayed power; and upon a throne that dwarfed all others sat Rāvaṇa himself, the ten-headed king, in the full majesty of his conquered worlds, magnificent and dreadful, the very image of sovereign power. It was a court meant to make any captive tremble, any petitioner shrink, any enemy despair; and into it Hanumān was led, bound with ropes, a single vānara amid all that arrayed demon might.

And Hanumān did not tremble.

This is the thing the chapter turns upon: that Hanumān, bound and alone in the heart of the enemy’s power, surrounded by the whole arrayed might of the demon race, standing before the conqueror of gods, was not overawed in the least, but stood there in his spirit entirely free, unbowed, unafraid, and looked upon Rāvaṇa and all his splendour with a calm and even a contempt that the demon king’s whole terrible majesty could not touch. His body was bound; his spirit was wholly free; and the freedom of his spirit in that place of overawing power is a kind of victory in itself, the victory of one who cannot be frightened by any display of might because his allegiance and his courage rest on something the enemy cannot reach.

Rāvaṇa demanded to know who he was and why he had come and dared to wreck the garden and slay the prince, and Hanumān answered, and his answer was bold beyond anything the court had ever heard addressed to their dread king. He declared himself the messenger of Rāma, and he delivered, there in the enemy’s own hall, before the whole assembled might of Lankā, a fierce and fearless warning and a demand.

I am the servant and envoy of Rāma, he told Rāvaṇa, prince of Ayodhyā, whose wife you have stolen by cowardly deceit, and I have come to find her, and I have found her, and I have seen what you have done, and I have come also to give you this warning, which you would be wise to heed. Return Sītā to Rāma. Return her now, with honour and with apology, and beg his forgiveness, and you may yet save yourself and your city and your race from the destruction you have called down. For Rāma is coming. He will cross your ocean; he will break your walls; he will destroy your armies and your champions and your sons; and he will kill you, Rāvaṇa, with all your ten heads, and lay your golden city in ash, unless you undo now, while there is still time, the crime you have committed. You have not captured a prize; you have embraced your doom. I have shown you today, in the wrecking of your garden and the slaying of your son and the breaking of your warriors, what a single servant of Rāma can do; imagine, then, what Rāma himself will do, and his whole army, when they come. Return Sītā, and live; keep her, and die, you and all your kind. That is the message I bring, and I have delivered it, and you would be a fool not to heed it.

It was an astonishing speech to be made by a bound captive to the conqueror of the gods in the midst of his own court, and it enraged Rāvaṇa past bearing, for no one addressed the lord of Lankā so, and to be so defied, so warned, so threatened, by a bound vānara in his own hall, was an insult his pride could not endure. In his fury he ordered Hanumān put to death on the spot, commanded that the insolent envoy be executed at once for his effrontery.

But here another voice was raised, and it was the voice of one of the few righteous souls in that court, and his intervention matters, for it introduces a figure who will become important. Rāvaṇa had a brother, Vibhīshaṇa, and Vibhīshaṇa, alone among the great ones of Lankā, was a soul inclined to righteousness, one who had always counselled his brother toward justice and away from the crime of Sītā’s abduction, one whose heart was set on dharma even amid the demon race. And Vibhīshaṇa now intervened to stop the execution, not out of love for Hanumān but out of respect for law and custom, for there was an ancient principle, honoured even among the demons, that an envoy, a messenger, was inviolable, that whatever his message and however offensive, a messenger must not be killed, for to kill the bearer of a message was a violation of the law of nations and a shameful act unworthy of a king. Do not kill him, brother, Vibhīshaṇa urged. He is an envoy, a messenger, and it is against all law and all custom to slay a messenger, however bold his words. Punish him if you must, but do not stain your honour and violate the sacred law by putting an envoy to death. It is beneath you and it is forbidden.

And Rāvaṇa, though enraged, heard his righteous brother, and could not simply ignore so fundamental a law, and so he relented from the execution, but he would not let the insolent envoy go unpunished, and he devised instead a punishment that was meant to humiliate, and that would prove, by the story’s grim irony, to be the instrument of Lankā’s burning. He would not kill the messenger; but a vānara, he knew, prized its tail, and so he ordered that Hanumān’s tail be wrapped in oil-soaked rags and set alight, and that the vānara be paraded so through the streets of the city with his tail burning, a humiliation, a mockery, a punishment meant to shame the bold envoy and send him home disgraced with his tail afire. So the order was given, and the demons seized Hanumān to carry it out, wrapping his tail in cloth and oil to make of it a torch; and in that vengeful and mocking punishment, Rāvaṇa, without knowing it, was placing in Hanumān’s own possession the fire that would consume his golden city.

Lankā in Flames

The demons wrapped Hanumān’s tail in oil-soaked rags, and the tellers say that the more they wrapped, the more Hanumān let his tail grow, lengthening it by his own power so that they had to use more and more cloth and more and more oil, until an enormous length of his tail was bound in fuel; and then they set it alight, and led him, tail blazing, through the streets of Lankā to be paraded and mocked before the whole city.

But before the fire could touch him or pain him, a wonder preserved him, and it came through Sītā. For word of Hanumān’s capture and punishment had reached the Ashokavana, and Sītā, hearing that the faithful messenger who had brought her Rāma’s ring and her first hope was being led with his tail afire through the city, was stricken with grief and fear for him, and she prayed. She prayed to Agni, the god of fire himself, with all the force of her fidelity and her virtue, that the fire should not burn Hanumān, that it should be cool to him, that the flames should spare the servant who had served her Lord so faithfully. And such was the power of Sītā’s virtue, of her unbroken chastity and devotion, that the fire-god heard her, and the fire on Hanumān’s tail, though it blazed and burned, gave him no pain and did him no harm; it was cool to him, harmless, for the prayer of so pure a soul had power even over fire. Hanumān felt the flames and knew that they did not burn him, and understood that some grace protected him, and his heart was glad.

And then Hanumān turned the punishment against those who had inflicted it, and here the story reaches one of its most spectacular and satisfying moments. His tail was ablaze, but the fire could not hurt him; he was bound, but his bonds were only ordinary ropes that his strength could break at will; and he was in the midst of the golden city of his enemy, a city of gold and wood, dry and rich and ready to burn. Hanumān saw his opportunity, and he took it. He broke his bonds, snapping the ropes as though they were threads, and he grew, swelling to a colossal size, and with his blazing tail he became a moving torch, a living instrument of fire loosed in the heart of a burnable city.

And he set Lankā ablaze. Leaping from rooftop to rooftop, from palace to palace, dragging his burning tail across the golden city, Hanumān set fire to Lankā, and the flames leapt up and spread and roared, catching the wooden mansions, the gilded pavilions, the great halls, the whole splendid fabric of the demon capital, until the golden city that Rāvaṇa had thought impregnable was a sea of flame, burning, collapsing, its splendour turned to roaring fire and rising smoke. Hanumān raced across the burning city, spreading the conflagration, and Lankā, the golden fortress, the seat of the demon power, the city that had never feared any enemy, burned from end to end in a single night at the hands of a single servant of Rāma.

Let us understand the full meaning of this burning, for it is not mere destruction, and the tellers weight it with significance. It was, first, the fulfillment of prophecy, for Trijaṭā had dreamed of Lankā in flames, and here the dream came true, the golden city burning exactly as the omen had foretold, the first great sign of the doom that was coming upon Rāvaṇa and all his kind. It was, second, the completion of Hanumān’s message written in destruction, for now Rāvaṇa and all Lankā had seen, beyond any possibility of doubt, what a single servant of Rāma could do: not merely wreck a garden or slay a prince, but burn their whole city to the ground. If one envoy could do this, what would the master and his army do? The burning was the ultimate demonstration, the final terrible warning, the proof written in fire across the whole city that Lankā’s doom was certain and coming. And it was, third, a kind of justice, the beginning of the repayment of all the wrongs that Lankā had done, the first installment of the destruction that Rāvaṇa had called down upon himself by his crime, the golden city beginning to pay, in fire, for the queen it held captive in its garden.

There is a grim irony in it that the tellers savour, and that we should savour too: that Rāvaṇa himself set this fire loose. It was his own vengeful, mocking punishment, the burning of the envoy’s tail, that put the fire into Hanumān’s possession and gave him the means to burn the city. Had Rāvaṇa simply killed Hanumān, or imprisoned him, or sent him away, Lankā would not have burned that night. But his pride demanded not merely to be rid of the insolent envoy but to humiliate him, to mock him, to send him home disgraced with his tail afire, and that vengeful excess, that need to humiliate rather than simply to punish, was exactly the thing that armed Hanumān with fire in the heart of the burnable city. Rāvaṇa’s own cruelty, his own vindictive pride, loosed the flames that consumed his capital. It is the pattern of the whole story of Rāvaṇa: that his own ungoverned passions, his lust, his pride, his vindictive cruelty, are the true authors of his ruin, that he destroys himself by his own excesses, that every cruelty he commits comes home to him magnified. He set a tail afire to mock an envoy, and burned his own golden city to the ground.

Amid the burning, Hanumān felt a sudden stab of fear, for he remembered Sītā, and dreaded that the fire he had loosed might spread to the Ashokavana and harm her. But he was reassured, whether by report or by his own reasoning or by a sign, that Sītā was safe, that the grove where she sat was spared, that the fire which he had loosed and which Sītā’s own prayer had made harmless to him had not touched the captive queen. And so, his work done, the city ablaze behind him, the warning delivered in fire, his errand complete beyond anything that had been asked of him, Hanumān quenched the fire of his tail in the sea, and prepared to make the great leap back across the ocean, to carry to Rāma the news that would end his grief and set the army in motion: that Sītā was found, that she lived and kept faith, that she waited, and that Lankā, for all its golden might, could be entered and wrecked and burned, and would fall.

A Carnival

Hanumān leapt back across the ocean, the hundred leagues that had seemed so impassable now crossed with the ease of a homecoming, and he came down upon the far shore where the anxious search party waited, and his coming was the signal for a joy that the tellers describe as a very carnival of gladness.

For the vānaras who had waited on the shore, who had sat in despair not so long before, preparing to die of failure, saw Hanumān returning across the sky, and they knew from his very bearing, before he had spoken a word, that he brought good news, that the errand had succeeded, that Sītā was found. And when he alighted among them and told them, told them that he had crossed the ocean and entered Lankā and found Sītā alive and faithful in the Ashokavana, that he had spoken with her and given her Rāma’s ring and received her token, that he had wrecked the demon’s garden and slain a prince and burned the golden city, the whole company erupted into a joy beyond containing. They leapt, they shouted, they embraced one another, they cheered until the shore rang with it. The despair of failure was transformed in an instant into the ecstasy of success, and the vānaras, who are by nature a merry and exuberant people, gave themselves wholly to a celebration as boisterous and unrestrained as their earlier despair had been deep.

And in the fullness of their joy, the tellers give us a delightful and very characteristic episode, small and merry amid the great matters, that shows the exuberant nature of the vānaras and lightens, for a moment, the gathering weight of the story before the war. For on their triumphant way back toward Kishkindhā, drunk with the joy of their success, the vānaras came upon the Madhuvana, the honey-garden, a great pleasure-grove of Sugrīva’s, a royal preserve full of honey and fruit, and they fell upon it in their exuberance and raided it. They gorged themselves on the honey, they feasted on the fruit, they grew merry and riotous and wholly out of hand, and when the keepers of the garden tried to stop them, the vānaras, in their high spirits and their sense that their triumph entitled them to any liberty, simply overwhelmed the keepers and went on with their revel, wrecking the royal honey-garden in a great disorderly carnival of celebration.

Now this was, strictly, a serious breach, for the Madhuvana was the king’s own preserve, and to raid it and rout its keepers was an offence against Sugrīva’s royal rights. And when word of it came to Sugrīva, that his honey- garden had been stormed and plundered by the returning search party, his first response might have been anger. But Sugrīva, hearing of it, understood at once what the raid on the Madhuvana meant, and his anger turned to joy, for he reasoned, shrewdly and correctly, that the search party would never have dared to raid his royal garden in such riotous high spirits unless their mission had succeeded, unless they were drunk with triumph as well as honey; that only the joy of success could account for such exuberant misrule; and that therefore the raid on the honey-garden was itself the happiest of news, the sign, before any messenger arrived, that Sītā had been found. Let them raid the garden, Sugrīva said in effect; their very misrule tells me they have succeeded; a search party that returns in defeat does not storm the king’s honey-garden in triumph. And so the breach was forgiven before it was even reproached, read rightly as the overflow of a joy too great to be contained, and the raid on the Madhuvana became not a crime to be punished but a sign to be celebrated.

There is a lightness in this episode that the story sets deliberately at this point, and it is worth appreciating, for the tellers know their craft. We stand at the threshold of the war, the great and terrible Yuddha Kāṇḍa, with all its slaughter and grief ahead; and just before we cross that threshold, the story gives us this: a carnival of joy, a riotous honey-feast, the merry misrule of the exuberant vānaras, a moment of pure gladness and even comedy before the darkness of the war descends. It is a breathing-space, a last lightness, the joy of the good news fully savoured before the heavy matters resume. And it is fitting, too, that this lightness should belong to the vānaras, the merry monkey-people, whose exuberance and warmth and high spirits are one of the story’s great pleasures, and who bring to the solemn epic a note of joy and even of comedy that humanizes it and lightens it and reminds us that even amid the greatest matters there is room for gladness, for celebration, for the simple animal joy of a triumph well earned and a honey-garden well raided.

So the search party came home at last to Kishkindhā and to the waiting Rāma, merry and triumphant, having found the lost queen and celebrated their finding with honey and misrule, and they brought with them the two things Rāma most needed: the certain news of where Sītā was, and the token, the Chūḍāmaṇi, that would prove the news true beyond any doubt. The great search that had begun in despair on the ocean shore, that had passed through Hanumān’s leap and Sītā’s finding and Lankā’s burning, ended now in this carnival of homecoming joy, and only one thing remained before the war could be set in motion: the delivering of the news, and the jewel, into Rāma’s own hands, and the ending, at last, of his long grief with the certain knowledge that his Sītā lived and waited and would be won back. And so the Sundara Kāṇḍa, the book of the flight of faith, the book that belongs above all to Hanumān and his great devoted deeds, draws toward its close, and the story turns from the finding of Sītā to the winning of her, from the leap of the single faithful servant to the march of the whole great army, from the flight of faith to the war of liberation.
